# Results — Study 468 (Gartley / AB=CD Harmonic)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a bullish
Gartley XABCD whose retracement ratios land on the Fibonacci grid (B = 0.618·XA, D = 0.786·XA)
marks a reversal at point D** — encoded as a mechanical rule. Pivots are confirmed fractals
(k = 4, with a 4-bar confirmation lag); at every confirmed swing-low we search recent pivots for
a valid bullish XABCD; a long fires at D-completion, entered at the **next close** (one documented
lag), and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **194** mechanical bullish-Gartley D-point completions pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 4) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal pivots usable only **+4 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per trade |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument pattern study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — D-point long vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch D-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = D − random.

| horizon | n | D-point | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (D−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 193 | +20.3 bps | 56% | +1.15 | +23.7 bps | **−3.4 bps** | +18.3 bps | −0.13 | 0.893 |
| 10-day | 193 | +57.2 bps | 67% | +2.01 | +39.6 bps | **+17.6 bps** | +55.2 bps | +0.47 | 0.641 |
| 20-day | 192 | +123.9 bps | 68% | +3.05 | +67.8 bps | **+56.2 bps** | +121.9 bps | +1.09 | 0.275 |
| 60-day | 189 | +275.9 bps | 70% | +3.57 | +75.2 bps | **+200.7 bps** | +273.9 bps | **+2.40** | **0.017** |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero rises with horizon (**+3.05** at 20d, **+3.57**
at 60d) — but much of that is **drift** that every long-only entry inherits. Against the
**drift-matched random baseline**, the D-point is a coin-flip at 5/10/20 days (Welch *t* = −0.13 /
+0.47 / +1.09, none clearing 2) and **only at 60 days does it clear the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar**
(Welch *t* = **+2.40**, *p* = 0.017, Δ = +201 bps). So there *is* a long-horizon effect — but read
the placebo before you call it Fibonacci.

| ticker | entries | D-point | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (D−random) |

| QQQ | 26 | +137.2 bps | +1.22 | +125.9 bps | **+11.3 bps** |
| IWM | 45 | +195.4 bps | +1.72 | +44.7 bps | **+150.7 bps** |
| DIA | 31 | −24.8 bps | −0.32 | +38.1 bps | **−63.0 bps** |
| GLD | 65 | +136.8 bps | +2.00 | +71.5 bps | **+65.3 bps** |

At 20 days the D-point beats random in 4 of 5 names but is negative on DIA; no single-ticker
*t* is decisive. At 60 days every per-ticker Δ is positive (+184 / +278 / +224 / +363 / +88 bps),
which is what lifts the pooled 60d Welch test over 2.

## Ratio-grid placebo — swap Fibonacci for random ratios, nothing changes

The decisive "do the **Fibonacci ratios** matter?" test: keep the entire XABCD zig-zag machinery
and the same tolerance band, but replace the Gartley targets (0.618 / 0.786) with **random** ratio
targets drawn from a plausible band. If price genuinely turns at *Fibonacci* D-points, the real
grid should beat almost every random grid.

| test | observed D-point return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY random-ratio grid, H = 20 | +132.8 bps | **0.443** | 500 |
| SPY random-ratio grid, H = 60 | +244.6 bps | **0.591** | 500 |

**44% (20d) / 59% (60d) of random ratio grids match or beat the Fibonacci grid.** The specific
0.618 / 0.786 numbers carry no information — any XABCD-shaped dip-buy at a confirmed swing low does
as well. The long-horizon edge is generic zig-zag dip-buying, **not** the Fibonacci ratios. "The
Fibonacci ratios forecast the D-point turn" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real Gartley bounce

On a deterministic tape with *planted* Gartley zig-zags followed by a real upward bounce (knob
`edge`), the same D-point rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat ratio result is a genuine
"the ratios aren't doing it", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | D-point | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 44 | −6.8 bps | 50% | −0.10 |
| **0.40** (real planted bounce) | 53 | +300.6 bps | 100% | **+60.63** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted Gartley
bounce lights up at *t* = +60.6 with a 100% win-rate. The detector is live and discriminating.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The D-point long beats a drift-matched random baseline **only at the 60-day
  horizon** (Welch *t* = +2.40, *p* = 0.017, Δ = +201 bps); at 5/10/20 days the touch is a coin
  flip (Welch *t* = −0.13 / +0.47 / +1.09, none ≥ 2). One horizon out of four clears the bar — a
  thin, long-only, long-horizon effect, not a robust signal.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The edge appears at a single 60-day horizon, vanishes at the shorter
  holds, and survives the geometry scramble — i.e. it is a *generic* "buy a confirmed swing low and
  wait three months" dip-buy, which you can capture far more cheaply without drawing forks. 194
  trades over 21 years is ~9/yr; costs eat into the thin shorter-horizon numbers; nothing scalable.
- **"Do the Fibonacci ratios forecast the D-point turn?" — BUSTED.** The ratio-grid placebo leaves
  the result intact (*p* = 0.44 at 20d, 0.59 at 60d): random ratio grids do as well as the
  Fibonacci grid, so the magic 0.618 / 0.786 numbers carry no forecasting information. Whatever
  long-horizon effect exists is swing-low dip-buying, not harmonic geometry.
